title: New York's 17th Congressional District Election, 2026
description: New York's 17th Congressional District, encompassing all of Rockland and Putnam counties and parts of northern Westchester and southeastern Dutchess counties, is one of the most competitive swing districts in the country. Incumbent Republican Rep. Mike Lawler, first elected in 2022 by unseating a Democratic incumbent, is seeking a third term in a district that Kamala Harris won in 2024. Democrats view this seat as a top pickup opportunity to help flip control of the House, with five candidates competing in the June 23, 2026 Democratic primary. The race centers on issues including the cost of living, the SALT deduction, abortion rights, and national security, with Lawler positioning himself as a moderate Republican while his Democratic challengers argue he has aligned too closely with the Trump administration.
polling_note: Limited public polling is available for this race. A Data for Progress poll from May 2026 showed Cait Conley leading the Democratic primary field. The Cook Political Report rates this race as a toss-up. Primary is June 23, 2026; general election polls are expected after the nominee is selected.

candidates.name: Michael Lawler
candidates.summary: Michael Lawler is the incumbent U.S. Representative for New York's 17th Congressional District, first elected in 2022. He advanced unopposed from the Republican primary and is running for a third term. Lawler represents a swing district and has positioned himself as a moderate Republican, emphasizing tax relief and bipartisan cooperation while supporting key elements of the Trump agenda.

candidates.name: Cait Conley
candidates.summary: Cait Conley is a fourth-generation Hudson Valley native, West Point graduate, and former Army Special Operations officer who served six overseas deployments and earned three Bronze Stars. She later served as Director for Counterterrorism on the National Security Council at the White House and worked at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). Conley is running as a moderate Democrat emphasizing national security experience, lowering costs, and protecting democratic institutions.

candidates.name: Beth Davidson
candidates.summary: Beth Davidson is a Rockland County Legislator and former Nyack School Board member who is running as a bipartisan problem-solver focused on lowering costs, protecting the environment, and keeping communities safe. She chairs the Environment Committee and serves as Vice Chair of the Housing and Economic Development Committee in the County Legislature. A two-time cancer survivor, Davidson emphasizes healthcare access and restoring the SALT deduction.

candidates.name: Effie Phillips-Staley
candidates.summary: Effie Phillips-Staley is a Tarrytown Village Trustee and nonprofit executive running as a progressive Democrat. Raised in a union household by a Salvadoran public school educator and a U.S. military veteran, she advocates for Medicare for All, universal childcare, building five million new homes, abolishing ICE, and Block the Bombs legislation. She is the endorsed Working Families Party nominee and refuses corporate PAC or AIPAC donations.

Cappello emphasizes his military background and commitment to putting country over party.

forecast.rationale: NY-17 remains a true toss-up with low confidence due to minimal direct general-election polling. The district is highly competitive — Kamala Harris won it in 2024, but Republican incumbent Mike Lawler has held the seat since 2022 and advanced unopposed through the GOP primary. The only available public poll (Data for Progress, May 2026) tests only the Democratic primary, showing Cait Conley (28%), Beth Davidson (24%), and Effie Phillips-Staley (16%) among three of five candidates, providing no head-to-head general-election evidence. Cook Political Report rates the race a toss-up. With the Democratic primary just three days away (June 23, 2026) and the nominee yet undetermined, the general-election picture is highly unsettled. Incumbency and Lawler's demonstrated crossover appeal give Republicans a narrow edge, but the Democratic presidential lean of the district and strong candidate field keep Democrats competitive. Until the nominee is chosen and general-election polling emerges, the race is a near-even toss-up with a slight edge to the incumbent.
